title: Make the export's settings file say what it means

blocks.text: The nightly report export reads a small settings file when it starts. Last month an operator set `export.batchsize=40` to ease the load on the database; the export ran with batches of 500 all week, and nobody knew until the database team asked. Another night the file was deployed without its `export.dir` line, and the reports were written to whatever directory the exporter happened to start in.
`ExportSettings.from(...)` already builds the settings from the three methods it calls. Finish the three `TODO`s in `src/main/java/practice/ExportSettings.java`, using `DEFAULTS` and `REQUIRED`.

When you're done, a file the exporter can use starts it, with the defaults filling in the optional settings the file leaves out. A file it can't use stops it with an `IllegalArgumentException` whose message names the setting at fault. About twelve lines in total.

cases.says: a file that sets every setting is read with its own values
an optional setting the file leaves out takes its default
a key the exporter doesn't know stops the start with its name, instead of leaving the setting it was meant for at its default
a missing required setting stops the start with its name; it gets no default
a value that doesn't parse stops the start with the setting's name, instead of falling back to the default

origin.section: A Default Also Hides a Misspelt Key, Unless Unknown Keys Stop the Start

concepts: An optional setting gets a default where a service running with it costs less than one refusing to start, as when a new release adds a key older config files lack; a setting with no safe value stays required.
A setting with no safe value stops the start when it is missing, instead of falling back to a guess.
A misspelt key leaves the setting it was meant for at its default without any error; refusing keys the loader doesn't know turns the typo into a failed start.
A value that doesn't parse is a failure, and a loader that catches it and uses the default hides it again.
